t.1.109.1: Janamejaya said: O best of those who know brahman, you have told of the excellent birth of the Dhārtarāṣṭras, a birth bestowed by a seer, superhuman though they were men.
t.1.109.2: And I have heard from you, O brahmin, the names of these as well, recounted one by one; but now tell me of the Pāṇḍavas.
t.1.109.4: Therefore I wish to hear of the birth of those men whose deeds surpassed the human; recount it all, Vaiśaṃpāyana.
t.1.109.3: For all of them, great-souled and possessing the prowess of the king of the gods, were proclaimed by you yourself, in the account of the descent of the partial incarnations, to be portions of the gods.
t.1.109.5: King Pāṇḍu, in a great wilderness, in a forest frequented by deer and beasts of prey, saw the leader of a herd of deer engaged in the act of mating.
t.1.109.6: Then Pāṇḍu pierced both that doe and him with five sharp, swift-flying arrows, gold-shafted and well-feathered.
t.1.109.7: And that son of a seer, O king, mighty in splendor, rich in austerities and full of energy, had united with his wife in the form of a deer.
t.1.109.8: But he, still joined with that doe, uttering a human voice, fell to the ground in an instant and lamented, his senses in turmoil.
t.1.109.10: Wisdom does not swallow up destiny, but destiny swallows up wisdom; wisdom cannot grasp the things that come about through destiny.
t.1.109.9: Even men overcome by desire and anger, even those bereft of the faculties of understanding, even men who delight in sin, refrain from cruel deeds.
t.1.109.11: O Bhārata, you were born in the foremost lineage of those whose selves are ever devoted to dharma; how is it that your mind, overcome by desire and greed, has strayed?
t.1.109.12: The conduct laid down for kings in the slaying of enemies is held to be the same for the slaying of deer. O deer, you should not reproach me out of delusion.
t.1.109.14: The seer Agastya, while seated at a sacrificial session, went hunting in the great forest, having sprinkled with consecrated water the wild animals dedicated to all the gods.
t.1.109.13: The slaying of deer, done without deceit and without trickery, is approved; that indeed is the dharma of kings. Knowing this, why then do you reproach me?
t.1.109.15: How can you reproach us, who act by a law established on authority? Through Agastya's sacrificial rite, your omentum was offered as an oblation.
t.1.109.18: I do not blame you, O king, for killing deer for your own sake; but out of compassion you ought here to have waited for my mating to be finished.
t.1.109.17: Whether the quarry be heedless or watchful, exposed in the open, men slay it by force, by stratagems, and with sharp arrows; why then, O deer, do you reproach me?
t.1.109.16: Indeed, men do not loose their arrows at enemies after first singling them out; rather, a moment of weakness in them is especially praised as the time for slaying.
t.1.109.19: At a time that is good for all beings and likewise desired by all beings, what wise man would kill a deer while it was mating in the forest? You have made vain that lovely fruit of man's purpose.
t.1.109.20: O Kauravya, this is not befitting of you, who were born in the lineage of the Pauravas and of those seers whose deeds were unwearied.
t.1.109.22: You who know the distinctions of the pleasures of women, who know the true meaning of the scriptures, of dharma and of artha, O you who resemble a god, ought not to do such a deed, which bars the way to heaven.
t.1.109.21: It is a cruel and exceedingly grave deed, condemned by all the worlds, one that does not lead to heaven, brings no glory, and is utterly unrighteous, O Bhārata.
t.1.109.23: O best of kings, men who commit cruel deeds and whose conduct is sinful, who have abandoned the three aims of life, are to be restrained by you.
t.1.109.24: What have you gained, best of men, by slaying me, a blameless sage who lives on roots and fruits, wearing the guise of a deer, O king, dwelling ever in the forests and wholly devoted to peace?
t.1.109.26: For I am the sage named Kiṃdama, unequalled in austerity; being ashamed before men, I engaged in sexual union with a doe.
t.1.109.27: Having become a deer, I roam with the deer in the dense forest. But this will not be the sin of killing a brahmin for you, since you acted unknowingly in slaying me, who wore the form of a deer and was thus overcome by desire.
t.1.109.25: Since I have been struck down by you, therefore without doubt a state that ends your life will come upon you too in just this way, you who wrought cruelty upon the two of us, helpless and deluded by desire.
t.1.109.28: But you, fool, shall surely reap a fruit just like this: deluded by desire, once you have come together with your beloved, you too shall go to the world of the dead in this very state.
t.1.109.29: At the hour of your death you will go to union with your beloved wife, and when you have fallen under the power of the king of the dead, which no creature can escape, that very woman, O best of the wise, will follow you out of devotion.
t.1.109.30: Just as I, while dwelling in happiness, was brought to sorrow by you, so sorrow will come upon you once happiness has been attained.
t.1.109.31: Having spoken thus, the deer, sorely afflicted with pain, was parted from life, and Pāṇḍu in an instant became stricken with grief.
